prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: Security advisories for affected dependencies (language en).
Grid: 5 columns × 7 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "CVE ID" · longest unbreakable word 46px · one-line width 125px
  col 2: header "Package" · longest unbreakable word 162px · one-line width 162px
  col 3: header "Affected versions" · longest unbreakable word 63px · one-line width 335px
  col 4: header "Severity" · longest unbreakable word 59px · one-line width 59px
  col 5: header "Summary" · longest unbreakable word 220px · one-line width 3094px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 720px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 719px.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

The image shows the table's content with every cell on one line, so you can read everything. Study it first.
1) Understand it: what is the table for, how will people read, scan and compare it, which columns play the same or similar role, which values must stay intact, which text may wrap naturally, and where existing row height could absorb wrapping.
2) Propose 3 genuinely different column-width designs for 720px (different strategies, not small variations).
Reply ONLY JSON: {"understanding":{"purpose":"","reading":"","groups":["columns that belong together and why"],"keep_intact":[""],"may_wrap":[""]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[int px per column, column 1 first],"idea":"one sentence"}]}

log.raw: {"understanding":{"purpose":"Help readers identify security advisories affecting dependencies, assess their severity, and understand the affected version ranges and issues.","reading":"Readers will scan CVE IDs and packages to find relevant advisories, then compare version ranges and severity before reading summaries; wrapped summaries can provide height for other cells to wrap within the same row.","groups":["CVE ID and Package identify the advisory and affected dependency.","Affected versions and Severity describe exposure and urgency; Summary explains the issue. Deeper summary wrapping can absorb wrapping elsewhere in the same row."],"keep_intact":["CVE IDs and package names should remain recognizable, especially long package paths.","Version numbers and comparison operators should stay together where possible.","Severity labels should remain on one line.","Long unbreakable terms in summaries need sufficient width or may be forced to break."],"may_wrap":["Affected version ranges can wrap between range clauses.","Summary prose can wrap naturally.","Headers can wrap where needed."]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[146,183,110,80,200],"idea":"Protect complete CVE IDs, package names and severity labels, accepting narrow version ranges and possible breaks in long summary terms."},{"name":"B","widths":[120,155,125,80,239],"idea":"Give the summary nearly enough space for its longest unbreakable term while sharing the remaining width across identifiers and version ranges."},{"name":"C","widths":[130,130,165,80,214],"idea":"Favor comparison of affected version ranges while allowing package names and summary text to wrap more aggressively."}]}
